content: Sal ammoniac is a rare mineral that consists of ammonium chloride (NH4Cl). It crystallizes in the isometric-hexoctahedral class, forming colorless, white, or yellow-brown crystals. The mineral exhibits very poor cleavage and has a brittle to conchoidal fracture. It is water-soluble and typically forms as encrustations created by sublimation around volcanic vents. Sal ammoniac is commonly found near volcanic fumaroles, guano deposits, and burning coal seams. Associated minerals include sodium alum, native sulfur, and other fumarole-related minerals. Notable occurrences of sal ammoniac include locations in Tajikistan, Mount Vesuvius in Italy, and Parícutin in Michoacán, Mexico. Historically, the term sal ammoniac was used to refer to the chemical compound ammonium chloride. The name originates from the Greek term ἅλς ἀμμωνιακός (hals ammoniakos), meaning salt of Ammon, due to its early production in Egypt. In modern applications, sal ammoniac is commonly used as a flux in the soldering of stained-glass windows. In jewelry-making and the refining of precious metals, potassium carbonate (cream of tartar) is added to gold and silver in a borax-coated crucible to purify iron or steel filings that may contaminate the scrap. Non-24-karat gold alloys, which contain silver and copper, often include small amounts of silica, zinc, and deoxidants to prevent porosity or cracking during the milling process. These additives are essential for producing high-quality ingots, especially when using traditional open crucible melting methods with a hand torch or blowpipe, as was done before the advent of electric melting furnaces. These traditional practices are still employed by metalsmiths and jewelers today. In the past, sal ammoniac was also used in bakery products to impart a crisp texture to cookies, although this application has largely fallen out of favor. However, in certain parts of Europe, particularly Scandinavia, it remains widely used in the production of salty licorice candy known as Salmiak. The term sal ammoniac has largely fallen out of general use during the 20th century.
